rationale: The BOOK ENTRY makes a lexical-referential claim: sabbath names the complete seven-unit (the week, and the seven at every scale the law counts), with the rest-day as the unit's completing member. Every material assertion printed in the entry is carried directly by the cited texts. Lev 23:15 counts 'seven sabbaths' that must be 'complete' (temimot), and the same omer count is given in Deut 16:9 as 'seven weeks' — a parallel statute equating shabbatot with shavuot for the identical span. Lev 25:2-8 runs the same word at year-scale ('a sabbath of rest unto the land'; 'seven sabbaths of years... forty and nine years'), which is only intelligible if sabbath names a countable unit, not a single day. The Greek assertions are verifiable and lexically uncontroversial: Luke 18:12's dis tou sabbatou means twice a week (no one fasts twice in one day), and Matt 28:1's mia sabbatōn ('one of the sabbaths') underlies every 'first day of the week,' with Matt 28:1 holding the day-sense and the unit-sense in one verse. Heb 4:9's sabbatismos supports 'crowned by rest' as the unit's completing member. The strongest counter — that sabbath names only the seventh-day and the week-usages are loose borrowings — either fails outright on Luke 18:12, Lev 25:8, and the Deut 16:9 parallel, or, in its metonymic form, concedes the entry's referent (the word does denote the week in these texts) and thus does not contradict the core. The entry is also compatible with, not a rival to, the common symbolic reading of rest in Christ; it defines what the word names, not what the rest typifies.
book_core_identification: Sabbath (shabbat/sabbaton) names the complete seven — the week itself and the seven-unit at every scale the law counts (seventh year, seven sevens to Jubilee) — with the day of rest as the completing member of that unit, not merely the name of a single rest-day.
book_secondary_elaborations: Hebrew counts the omer span as 'seven sabbaths' (shabbatot, Lev 23:15) where Deuteronomy counts the same span as 'seven weeks' (shavuot, Deut 16:9), equating the terms by parallel statute.
Greek calls the week the sabbath: dis tou sabbatou (Luke 18:12) means twice a week, and every 'first day of the week' is literally mia sabbatōn, 'one of the sabbaths' (Matt 28:1).
The unit scales: the land's seventh year is a sabbath, and Jubilee is reached by counting 'seven sabbaths of years' (Lev 25:2-8).
The rest is the completing member of the whole unit (Heb 4:9).
chapter_only_objections: The lunar-anchored calendar reconstruction (months built of four sevens with sabbaths fixed on the 8th, 15th, 22nd, and 29th, and renewed-moon days outside the sevens) is a contested chapter-level claim not asserted in the entry and not adjudicated here.
The prophetic scaling of the sabbath to a 7,000-year 'great week' with a millennial seventh via 2 Peter 3:8 and Heb 4:9-11 is a chapter-only typological application.

The argument that temimot ('complete') would be a dead word on a continuous weekly cycle, and the resulting resolution of the omer-count 'checksum,' depends on the chapter's calendar thesis rather than on the entry's lexical claim.
The claim that 'rest is not the absence of work; it is whose work fills the day' (from Isa 58:13, John 5:17, Num 28:9) is chapter-level exposition beyond the entry.
strongest_counter_interpretation: Sabbath properly and primarily names only the seventh-day rest itself; occurrences like 'seven sabbaths' count seven rest-days rather than seven week-spans, and the Greek usage of sabbaton for 'week' is a later, loose semantic extension (metonymy from the day to the span it closes) rather than the biblical meaning of the word — so the glossary should define the term as the rest-day, with any week-sense treated as derivative idiom.
counter_core_identification: Sabbath = the seventh-day of rest only; week-denoting occurrences are secondary idiom, not part of what the word names.
material_core_denial: The counter denies that sabbath names the seven-unit at all: it asserts the word's referent is exclusively the single rest-day, so 'seven sabbaths' means seven rest-days and the week-sense in Greek is a post-biblical extension carrying no definitional weight.
counter_case: Conduct laws unambiguously attach sabbath to a single day: kindle no fire, the offering of the day, 'remember the sabbath day' (Exod 20:8).
The creation account grounds the word in the seventh day alone, on which God rested (Gen 2:2-3).
Naming a span by its marked day is common calendar idiom (as Passover names the whole feast week, Luke 22:1), so week-usages could be metonymy from the day's name rather than the word's own meaning.
Ezekiel 46:1 and Exod 20:8 speak of 'the day of the sabbath,' which the counter reads as simple apposition, sabbath being the day.
book_explanatory_advantages: Luke 18:12's dis tou sabbatou is fatal to the day-only reading: no one fasts twice in a single day; the Pharisee calls the seven 'the sabbath.'

Lev 25:8's 'seven sabbaths of years... forty and nine years' requires sabbath to be a countable span-unit (a seven of years), not a day; a day-only lexicon cannot produce 49 years from seven rest-days.

The Lev 23:15 / Deut 16:9 parallel statute renders the identical count as 'seven sabbaths' and 'seven weeks,' equating the terms by Scripture's own cross-witness — exactly the two-witness method the book's introduction establishes.
Lev 23:15's temimot ('complete/whole') fits a span that can be whole or broken; a day cannot be partially itself.
Matt 28:1 holds both senses in one verse ('end of the sabbath... one of the sabbaths'), which the entry's unit-plus-marked-day account explains and the day-only account must treat as equivocation.

The genitive constructions 'day of the sabbath' (Exod 20:8; Ezek 46:1, paralleling 'day of the new moon,' where chodesh undisputedly names the month-unit) are redundant if sabbath names only a day and exact if the unit owns a marked day.

The entry's account is compatible with the metonymic-origin story: even if the week-sense arose by extension from the day, the cited biblical texts demonstrably use the word for the unit, which is all the entry asserts.
counter_explanatory_advantages: The counter matches the most familiar usage: conduct laws, creation rest, and ordinary translation all foreground the single day.
It requires no revision of common lexical intuition and aligns with how most English versions render sabbaton in the resurrection accounts ('week' being treated as idiom).
decisive_sources: Leviticus 23:15 with Deuteronomy 16:9 (identical count named 'seven sabbaths' and 'seven weeks')
Leviticus 25:8 ('seven sabbaths of years... forty and nine years')
Luke 18:12 (dis tou sabbatou — 'twice in the week')
Matthew 28:1 (day-sense and mia sabbatōn unit-sense in one verse)
Hebrews 4:9 (the rest as the remaining/completing member)
unresolved_objections: Whether the week-sense is the word's primary meaning or a metonymic extension of the day's name is not settled by the cited texts; the entry's claims hold either way, but the stronger definitional priority ('was never a day's name') argued in the chapter is not adjudicated here.
The chapter's calendrical reconstruction (fixed monthly sabbaths) remains contested and is outside the entry's scope.
